claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by interface-mediated dislocation climb.
Severe lattice distortion and differences in short-range order between alternating FCC and BCC layers enhance interface-mediated dislocation climb.
FCC/BCC interfaces create localized coherency stresses.
The interfaces initially act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Under sustained loading, the interfaces eventually promote dislocation climb and accumulation.
Interface-mediated climb produces accelerated creep relative to a homogeneous microstructure.
The proposed starting material is a nanoscale coating containing alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
Constant-stress tests at room temperature and approximately 500–600 °C should compare the multilayer with a homogeneous HEA having the same overall composition.
Differences in lattice parameter and short-range order across nanoscale FCC/BCC interfaces generate coherency stresses that locally modulate dislocation mobility.
Dislocations initially pile up at multilayer interfaces because of incoherency and lattice distortion.
Stress concentrations at interfacial barriers promote dislocation climb through lattice diffusion.
The multilayer and homogeneous samples will initially have similar deformation rates, after which the multilayer rate will become increasingly accelerated.
The multilayer will develop higher local dislocation densities at its interfaces than are found in the homogeneous control.
A homogeneous HEA of comparable overall composition has fewer coherency-induced barriers than the nanoscale multilayer.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the nanoscale multilayer architecture remains intact.
Diffusion-assisted dislocation climb is activated in moderate-to-elevated temperature regimes below phase-transformation thresholds.
The exact creep acceleration and the quantitative contribution of climb relative to other mechanisms are uncertain.
Interrupted creep testing with TEM and EBSD can compare interfacial dislocation structures in multilayer and homogeneous samples.
Diffusion markers or void formation observed by high-resolution microscopy would constitute evidence of dislocation climb.
Failure to observe either accelerated multilayer creep or increased interfacial dislocation accumulation would falsify the proposed interface-mediated-climb mechanism.
